title: Comparative Plant Anatomy
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 400L Plant Science comparative anatomy curriculum: meristems and primary growth, tissue systems (dermal, ground, vascular), primary structure of root/stem/leaf in monocots and dicots, secondary growth and wood anatomy, comparative anatomy across pteridophytes/gymnosperms/angiosperms, and adaptive (ecological) anatomy.

questions.question: Apical meristems are located at:
options: The tips of roots and shoots
Scattered randomly throughout the plant body
questions.correct_answer: The tips of roots and shoots
questions.explanation: Apical meristems occur at root and shoot tips and are responsible for primary growth (increase in length).

questions.question: According to the histogen theory of Hanstein, the root/shoot apical meristem is organised into three layers. Which layer gives rise to the epidermis?
questions.correct_answer: Dermatogen
questions.explanation: In Hanstein's histogen theory, the dermatogen is the outermost layer that differentiates into the epidermis; the periblem forms the cortex and the plerome forms the central vascular cylinder.

questions.question: The tunica-corpus theory of shoot apical organisation, unlike the histogen theory, distinguishes zones primarily on the basis of:
questions.correct_answer: Plane of cell division
questions.explanation: In the tunica-corpus concept the tunica layers divide anticlinally (maintaining surface layers) while the corpus divides in various planes, contributing to bulk growth -- a distinction based on division plane rather than fixed cell lineages.

questions.question: Which of the following is a lateral meristem responsible for secondary growth in girth?
questions.correct_answer: Vascular cambium
questions.explanation: The vascular cambium and cork cambium are lateral meristems that produce secondary xylem/phloem and periderm respectively, increasing stem/root girth.

questions.question: Intercalary meristems, found at the base of internodes in grasses, are responsible for:
options: Rapid elongation of the internode/leaf base after the apex has matured
questions.correct_answer: Rapid elongation of the internode/leaf base after the apex has matured
questions.explanation: Intercalary meristems are remnants of apical meristem left behind at internode or leaf bases (typical of grasses) and allow rapid regrowth, e.g. after grazing or mowing.

questions.question: The epidermis of leaves and young stems is typically covered externally by a waxy, water-repellent layer called the:
questions.correct_answer: Cuticle
questions.explanation: The cuticle is a lipid (cutin and wax) layer secreted by epidermal cells that reduces water loss and protects against pathogens.

questions.question: Stomata are surrounded by specialised epidermal cells called guard cells, whose change in turgor pressure controls:
options: The size of the stomatal pore for gas exchange and transpiration
Cell division rate in the cambium
questions.correct_answer: The size of the stomatal pore for gas exchange and transpiration
questions.explanation: Guard cells swell or shrink in response to turgor changes, opening or closing the stomatal pore to regulate CO2/O2 exchange and water vapour loss.

questions.question: In a typical dicotyledonous leaf, stomata are most abundant on the:
questions.correct_answer: Lower (abaxial) epidermis
questions.explanation: Most dorsiventral dicot leaves are hypostomatic, with stomata concentrated on the lower surface to minimise water loss from the sun-exposed upper surface.

questions.question: Trichomes (epidermal hairs) can function to:
options: Reduce water loss, reflect excess light and deter herbivores
Store starch as the main plant reserve
questions.correct_answer: Reduce water loss, reflect excess light and deter herbivores
questions.explanation: Trichomes are epidermal outgrowths that variously reduce transpiration by trapping a boundary layer of humid air, reflect light, and physically or chemically deter herbivory.

questions.question: Which simple ground tissue is characterised by living cells with thin primary walls, retains the capacity to divide, and forms the bulk of cortex and pith?
questions.correct_answer: Parenchyma
questions.explanation: Parenchyma cells are living, thin-walled and metabolically active, functioning in photosynthesis, storage and wound repair, and retain totipotency.

questions.question: Collenchyma differs from parenchyma mainly in that collenchyma:
options: Has unevenly thickened primary walls and provides flexible mechanical support in growing organs
questions.correct_answer: Has unevenly thickened primary walls and provides flexible mechanical support in growing organs
questions.explanation: Collenchyma cells are living but have unevenly thickened, non-lignified primary walls, giving flexible support to young stems and petioles that are still elongating.

questions.question: Sclerenchyma cells provide rigid mechanical support because they:
options: Have thick lignified secondary walls and are usually dead at maturity
questions.correct_answer: Have thick lignified secondary walls and are usually dead at maturity
questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma (fibres and sclereids) develops thick, lignified secondary walls that provide rigid, permanent mechanical strength once the cell has lost its protoplast.

questions.question: Sclereids differ from fibres in that sclereids are typically:
options: Long and thin, arranged in bundles for tensile strength
Short, variously shaped cells (e.g. stone cells) that provide localised hardness, as in pear fruit grit cells
questions.correct_answer: Short, variously shaped cells (e.g. stone cells) that provide localised hardness, as in pear fruit grit cells
questions.explanation: Sclereids are short, often isodiametric or branched sclerenchyma cells (e.g. brachysclereids/stone cells) giving hardness to seed coats, nut shells and fruit flesh, unlike the long, tapering fibres.

questions.question: Which xylem conducting element is characteristic of angiosperms but generally absent in most gymnosperms?
questions.correct_answer: Vessel elements
questions.explanation: Vessel elements, joined end-to-end into long vessels via perforation plates, are the main water-conducting cells of most angiosperms; gymnosperm xylem conducts mainly through tracheids (Gnetum being a notable exception).

questions.question: Tracheids differ from vessel elements in that tracheids:
options: Have perforation plates connecting them end to end
Are imperforate and conduct water laterally through pits between overlapping tapered ends
questions.correct_answer: Are imperforate and conduct water laterally through pits between overlapping tapered ends
questions.explanation: Tracheids are elongated, tapering, dead cells lacking perforation plates; water moves between them through bordered pits, whereas vessel elements have open perforation plates allowing more efficient axial flow.

questions.question: In the phloem, the living cells that conduct organic solutes (sugars) through sieve areas/sieve plates are the:
questions.correct_answer: Sieve tube elements
questions.explanation: Sieve tube elements are the conducting cells of angiosperm phloem, connected end to end through sieve plates, and are associated with companion cells that maintain their metabolic activity.

questions.question: Companion cells are closely associated with sieve tube elements because:
options: Sieve tube elements lack a nucleus at maturity and depend on companion cells for metabolic support and loading/unloading of solutes
They replace sieve tubes in gymnosperms
They conduct water instead of sugars
They are found only in roots
questions.correct_answer: Sieve tube elements lack a nucleus at maturity and depend on companion cells for metabolic support and loading/unloading of solutes
questions.explanation: Mature sieve tube elements lose their nucleus and much of their organelle content; companion cells, connected by numerous plasmodesmata, supply ATP and help with phloem loading and unloading.

questions.question: Gymnosperm phloem lacks companion cells but instead has functionally analogous cells called:
questions.correct_answer: Albuminous cells
questions.explanation: In gymnosperms the conducting cells are sieve cells (not sieve tubes) and albuminous cells (often derived from ray or axial parenchyma) perform a companion-cell-like nutritive role.

questions.question: In a typical dicotyledonous root in transverse section, the arrangement of primary xylem is:
options: Exarch (protoxylem towards the periphery, metaxylem towards the centre), with a solid, usually 2-4 armed (diarch to tetrarch) star-shaped xylem core
Endarch with xylem in a ring around the pith
Scattered in bundles as in monocot stems
questions.correct_answer: Exarch (protoxylem towards the periphery, metaxylem towards the centre), with a solid, usually 2-4 armed (diarch to tetrarch) star-shaped xylem core
questions.explanation: Root xylem is exarch, maturing centripetally, and in dicot roots typically forms a solid star-shaped core (di- to polyarch) at the very centre, unlike the endarch xylem of stems.

questions.question: The single layer of cells surrounding the vascular cylinder (stele) in the root, characterised by Casparian strips, is the:
questions.correct_answer: Endodermis
questions.explanation: The endodermis is the innermost cortical layer, with suberised/lignified Casparian strips in its radial and transverse walls that force water and solutes through the symplast, regulating entry into the stele.

questions.question: Lateral roots originate from which tissue layer?
questions.correct_answer: Pericycle
questions.explanation: Lateral roots arise endogenously from the pericycle, a meristematic layer just inside the endodermis, which is why lateral roots must grow through the cortex and epidermis to emerge.

questions.question: A key anatomical difference between typical monocot and dicot roots is that monocot roots usually have:
options: No secondary growth and a pith at the centre, with polyarch xylem
questions.correct_answer: No secondary growth and a pith at the centre, with polyarch xylem
questions.explanation: Monocot roots typically retain a central pith (rather than solid xylem core) with numerous (polyarch) xylem bundles arranged around it, and lack a vascular cambium so they do not undergo secondary thickening.

questions.question: In a typical dicotyledonous stem, the vascular bundles are arranged as:
options: A single ring of open, collateral bundles separating cortex from pith
Scattered bundles throughout the ground tissue
Concentric bundles with xylem surrounding phloem
questions.correct_answer: A single ring of open, collateral bundles separating cortex from pith
questions.explanation: Dicot stems typically show a ring of open collateral vascular bundles (each with cambium between xylem and phloem), delimiting an outer cortex from an inner pith.

questions.question: A characteristic feature distinguishing typical monocot stems from dicot stems is that monocot stems have:
options: Vascular bundles scattered throughout the ground tissue and are usually closed (no cambium)
A single ring of open bundles
A prominent vascular cambium producing annual rings
questions.correct_answer: Vascular bundles scattered throughout the ground tissue and are usually closed (no cambium)
questions.explanation: Monocot stems (e.g. maize) have numerous scattered closed collateral vascular bundles lacking cambium, so most monocots do not show secondary growth, unlike the ring arrangement in dicots.

questions.question: In a collateral vascular bundle, the relative position of xylem and phloem is:
options: Xylem and phloem lie side by side on the same radius, with xylem towards the centre and phloem towards the periphery
Xylem and phloem alternate around the bundle
questions.correct_answer: Xylem and phloem lie side by side on the same radius, with xylem towards the centre and phloem towards the periphery
questions.explanation: Collateral bundles, the commonest type in angiosperms, have phloem located only on the outer (abaxial) side of the xylem along a single radius.

questions.question: Bicollateral vascular bundles, found in families such as Cucurbitaceae and Solanaceae, differ from ordinary collateral bundles by having:
options: Phloem on both the outer and inner sides of the xylem
Xylem on both sides of the phloem
questions.correct_answer: Phloem on both the outer and inner sides of the xylem
questions.explanation: Bicollateral bundles have an additional strand of internal (intraxylary) phloem on the inner side of the xylem, in addition to the usual external phloem.

questions.question: A dorsiventral (bifacial) leaf, typical of most dicots, shows internal differentiation into:
options: Palisade mesophyll towards the upper surface and spongy mesophyll towards the lower surface
Palisade mesophyll on both surfaces equally
questions.correct_answer: Palisade mesophyll towards the upper surface and spongy mesophyll towards the lower surface
questions.explanation: Dorsiventral leaves are structurally and functionally different on their two surfaces, with compact, chloroplast-rich palisade cells adaxially and loosely arranged spongy mesophyll with large air spaces abaxially.

questions.question: Isobilateral (isolateral) leaves, common in many monocots such as grasses growing vertically, show:
options: Palisade mesophyll on both surfaces (or none at all), with stomata on both surfaces
Palisade only on the lower surface
Xylem and phloem fused into one tissue
questions.correct_answer: Palisade mesophyll on both surfaces (or none at all), with stomata on both surfaces
questions.explanation: Because isobilateral leaves are oriented vertically and receive similar light on both faces, mesophyll differentiation and stomatal distribution tend to be similar on both surfaces.

questions.question: Kranz anatomy, seen in the leaves of C4 plants such as maize and sugarcane, is characterised by:
options: Ordinary mesophyll only, with no bundle sheath
A distinct wreath-like arrangement of enlarged, chloroplast-rich bundle sheath cells surrounding the vascular bundle, with radiating mesophyll cells
Total absence of vascular bundles in the leaf
Palisade cells replacing bundle sheath cells
questions.correct_answer: A distinct wreath-like arrangement of enlarged, chloroplast-rich bundle sheath cells surrounding the vascular bundle, with radiating mesophyll cells
questions.explanation: Kranz ("wreath") anatomy is the hallmark of C4 photosynthesis: enlarged bundle-sheath cells with numerous chloroplasts encircle each vascular bundle, closely associated with radiating mesophyll cells, enabling the two-cell C4 carbon-concentrating pathway.

questions.question: Secondary growth in dicot stems and roots results mainly from the activity of two lateral meristems, namely:
questions.correct_answer: Vascular cambium and cork cambium (phellogen)
questions.explanation: The vascular cambium produces secondary xylem and phloem, while the cork cambium (phellogen) produces the periderm (cork, phellogen, phelloderm) that replaces the epidermis in girth-increasing organs.

questions.question: The vascular cambium produces secondary xylem and secondary phloem by dividing:
options: Periclinally (parallel to the surface), cutting off xylem to the inside and phloem to the outside
Randomly in all planes with no pattern
Only towards the pith, never towards the cortex
questions.correct_answer: Periclinally (parallel to the surface), cutting off xylem to the inside and phloem to the outside
questions.explanation: Cambial initials divide periclinally, adding secondary xylem cells centripetally (inward) and secondary phloem cells centrifugally (outward), while occasional anticlinal divisions increase the cambium's circumference.

questions.question: Annual growth rings in temperate tree wood arise because:
options: The cambium produces distinctly different-sized xylem cells in spring (earlywood, wider lumen) versus summer/autumn (latewood, narrower, thicker-walled cells) each growing season
Each ring represents one month of growth
The pith adds a new layer every year
Rings are formed only in tropical evergreen trees
questions.correct_answer: The cambium produces distinctly different-sized xylem cells in spring (earlywood, wider lumen) versus summer/autumn (latewood, narrower, thicker-walled cells) each growing season
questions.explanation: Seasonal changes in cambial activity produce earlywood with larger, thinner-walled vessels/tracheids and denser latewood, and the visible contrast between one season's latewood and the next season's earlywood marks each annual ring.

questions.question: The dark-coloured, non-conducting central wood of an old tree trunk, impregnated with resins, tannins and gums, is called:
questions.correct_answer: Heartwood
questions.explanation: Heartwood is the older, physiologically inactive inner wood whose vessels become blocked (e.g. by tyloses) and infiltrated with extractives, giving it darker colour and greater durability, while the outer, still-conducting sapwood remains lighter.

questions.question: Wood in which the vessels are more or less uniform in diameter and evenly distributed throughout a growth ring is described as:
questions.correct_answer: Diffuse-porous
questions.explanation: Diffuse-porous wood has vessels of relatively similar size scattered evenly through the growth ring (e.g. many tropical hardwoods), in contrast to ring-porous wood where large earlywood vessels form a distinct band.

questions.question: In roots and stems, ray cells (vascular rays) function mainly to:
options: Conduct water and photosynthate radially and store food
Photosynthesise as the main leaf tissue
questions.correct_answer: Conduct water and photosynthate radially and store food
questions.explanation: Rays are radially oriented strips of parenchyma that cross the secondary xylem and phloem, providing lateral (radial) transport and storage of food reserves.

questions.question: The bark of a woody stem, in the general (non-technical) sense, includes all tissues:
options: Outside the vascular cambium, i.e. secondary phloem plus periderm
Only the outer dead cork layer
questions.correct_answer: Outside the vascular cambium, i.e. secondary phloem plus periderm
questions.explanation: In common usage, "bark" refers to everything external to the vascular cambium: the living secondary phloem (inner bark) and the periderm/cork (outer bark).

questions.question: Lenticels, small pores visible on the bark of woody stems, function to:
options: Allow gas exchange through the periderm after the epidermis and stomata are lost
questions.correct_answer: Allow gas exchange through the periderm after the epidermis and stomata are lost
questions.explanation: Lenticels are loosely arranged masses of cells (complementary cells) in the periderm that permit gaseous exchange between internal living tissues and the atmosphere once the epidermis is replaced by cork.

questions.question: Anomalous secondary growth, seen in some lianas and a few dicot families, may involve:
options: Formation of successive rings of cambium producing interxylary phloem (included phloem)
Complete absence of any vascular tissue
Only primary growth throughout the plant's life
Loss of the ability to photosynthesise
questions.correct_answer: Formation of successive rings of cambium producing interxylary phloem (included phloem)
questions.explanation: Some climbers and a few tree genera (e.g. Boerhavia, Bignoniaceae lianas) show anomalous secondary growth patterns, such as successive cambial rings that embed strands of phloem within the xylem (included/interxylary phloem), differing from the normal single-cambium pattern.

questions.question: Stem anatomy of pteridophytes such as ferns typically shows a stele called a:
options: Protostele or siphonostele, without true secondary growth in most living ferns
A stele with annual growth rings
questions.correct_answer: Protostele or siphonostele, without true secondary growth in most living ferns
questions.explanation: Ferns (pteridophytes) typically possess simple stelar types such as protosteles or siphonosteles (or dictyosteles), and most living ferns lack a vascular cambium, so they do not undergo secondary thickening like seed plants.

questions.question: Gymnosperm wood is described as "homoxylous" or "non-porous" because it consists almost entirely of:
options: Tracheids, lacking true vessels (in most conifers)
questions.correct_answer: Tracheids, lacking true vessels (in most conifers)
questions.explanation: Most gymnosperm (conifer) wood is composed almost entirely of tracheids performing both conduction and support, without the vessel elements that characterise angiosperm (hardwood) xylem.

questions.question: Hydrophytes (aquatic plants) typically show which anatomical adaptation?
options: Well-developed aerenchyma with large air spaces and reduced xylem/lignification
Thick cuticle and sunken stomata to reduce water loss
Extensive root hairs for water absorption
Very high proportion of sclerenchyma for rigidity
questions.correct_answer: Well-developed aerenchyma with large air spaces and reduced xylem/lignification
questions.explanation: Submerged and floating aquatic plants develop aerenchyma (large intercellular air spaces) for buoyancy and internal gas transport, and since water provides physical support and is not limiting, xylem and mechanical tissue are correspondingly reduced.

questions.question: Xerophytes (plants of dry habitats) commonly show which anatomical feature to reduce transpirational water loss?
options: Thick cuticle, sunken stomata in pits/crypts, and reduced leaf surface area
Thin cuticle and stomata raised above the leaf surface
Large intercellular air spaces filling most of the leaf
questions.correct_answer: Thick cuticle, sunken stomata in pits/crypts, and reduced leaf surface area
questions.explanation: Xerophytic adaptations that minimise water loss include a thick waxy cuticle, stomata sunken in pits or hairy crypts (creating a humid microenvironment), reduced leaf area, and often a well-developed water-storage (succulent) tissue.

questions.question: In preparing plant tissue for microscopic anatomical study, the standard sequence of steps typically includes:
options: Fixation, dehydration, embedding, sectioning (microtomy) and staining
Only staining, with no other preparation needed
Germination, flowering and fruiting of the whole plant
Freezing the whole organ without sectioning
questions.correct_answer: Fixation, dehydration, embedding, sectioning (microtomy) and staining
questions.explanation: Standard plant anatomical technique preserves tissue structure by fixation, then removes water by dehydration, embeds the tissue (e.g. in paraffin wax) for support, cuts thin sections with a microtome, and stains sections to visualise different tissues (e.g. safranin-fast green for lignified vs cellulosic walls).

questions.question: The double staining technique using safranin and fast green (or light green) on plant sections is used mainly to distinguish:
options: Lignified tissues (stained red/pink by safranin) from cellulosic, non-lignified tissues (stained green)
Living cells from dead cells only
questions.correct_answer: Lignified tissues (stained red/pink by safranin) from cellulosic, non-lignified tissues (stained green)
questions.explanation: Safranin selectively stains lignified and suberised walls (xylem, sclerenchyma) red/pink, while fast green/light green counterstains cellulosic walls (parenchyma, phloem) green, allowing tissues to be distinguished under the microscope.

questions.question: A tangential longitudinal section (TLS) of wood, cut at right angles to the rays, is useful for observing:
options: The height and width of rays as seen from the side, and vessel arrangement along the grain
Only the transverse arrangement of growth rings
questions.correct_answer: The height and width of rays as seen from the side, and vessel arrangement along the grain
questions.explanation: A tangential section, cut perpendicular to the rays, shows rays in end/side view (revealing their height and width) together with the longitudinal extent of axial elements such as vessels and fibres, complementing information from transverse and radial sections.

questions.question: The pith is the ground tissue located:
options: At the very centre of a typical dicot stem, surrounded by the ring of vascular bundles
In the outermost layer of the root
Between the vascular cambium and the phloem
questions.correct_answer: At the very centre of a typical dicot stem, surrounded by the ring of vascular bundles
questions.explanation: The pith is central parenchymatous ground tissue enclosed by the ring of vascular bundles in a typical dicot stem, often functioning in storage.
